messages.subject: Re: ice on transect ?
parts:
Dear Colleagues,

Thanks for the discussion, very interesting.

I share the views on ice not affecting much the actual
detectability as such; but what about the true 'area surveyed' (open
water) and the actual density estimate + extrapolations of these
densities to ice free or ice covered areas (=populations)?

How big is the difference really between


Density = Birds/full area surveyed (ice area included)

vs.

Density = Birds/ice free area surveyed (ice area excluded)


If ice coverage makes areas unavailable to birds, doesn't this
create problems in the density value (area used for division) and in the
overall population estimate for a region ?

The issue is that ice during a survey can change largely and too
quickly.
I was suggested the use of a ice-recording video camera, which might be
a solution.

Thanks for the info and earlier discussion; yours

F.

Rod's caveats brings up some interesting points about 1.) stratification
and 2.) heterogeneity in detection probability. I hope to hear more
discussion. Somebody steer me back on course.

1.) Stratification by areas with more ice, even if it is 8/10 of the
length, is not necessary. That is, estimates are unbiased. However
stratification may, under some circumstances, increase precision.
Specifically, this will only be a large benefit when lines vary in the
amount of ice they traverse. Perhaps a ratio estimator would perform
better anyway(?) - in which case you are back to simply exluding the ice
areas and using shortened line lengths. Why stratify?

2.) The second and third concerns listed by Rod (whether ice affect
detectability through sighting conditions or animal behavior) are
factors
that induce heterogeneity in individual detection probability. "Pooling
robustness" or approximate robustness should negate this as a critical
concern (?). Assuming there is no sample bias (eg, to avoid ice edges)
I
do not see any problem if ice does indeed affect animal behavior or
detectability. These factors are already highly variable across a study
area anyway. It seems to me that pooling robustness is not well
understood, myself included. Can anyone provide some insight?

These are difficulties that I often hear about in designing distance
surveys, and I think many of them are unnecessary. Specifically, the
properties of random samples and pooling robust modeling allow for our
ignorance every possible factor affecting density or detectability. Any
thoughts?

Cheers,
~aaron

I agree with Jeff that if the ice represents random patches of zero
density
then you should be able to proceed with the analysis, ignoring the ice.
However, you should consider the possible impact of ice on the survey,
for
instance:
1) Did ice impact the survey design? Not just dodging the occasional
berg
but say your survey tracks were all <3/10 ice but your study area
included
8/10 ice then you may need to stratify your data.
2) Does the ice affect the observations? By creating visual contrast or
acting as cue.
3) Do the birds behave differently in the area around ice or in
different
densities of ice? e.g. resting on or near ice and foraging in open
water.

Rod

messages.subject: Re: ice on transect ?
parts:
> > Density = Birds/full area surveyed (ice area included)
> >
> > vs.
> >
> > Density = Birds/ice free area surveyed (ice area excluded)
> >
> >
> > If ice coverage makes areas unavailable to birds, doesn't this
> > create problems in the density value (area used for division) and in the
> > overall population estimate for a region ?

Falk, if there are no birds in the areas covered by ice, the problem is
simple in principle. You can adopt 2 strategies. In the first, you
simply exclude the ice covered areas, and treat it as a survey of the
remainder. Then the density estimate is an estimate for areas without
ice.

In the second, you include areas covered by ice, include the effort you
would have expended, had you been able to survey the ice sections, and
assume that you would have recorded no birds on these sections. In this
case, the density estimate is an average for the whole area, including
ice.

In either case, if you multiply the density estimate by the appropriate
area (without or with ice), you will get virtually the same abundance
estimate.

The second strategy does not need you to estimate what proportion of the
area is covered with ice.

A complication arises if survey effort is conducted when you are skirting
around the ice, on the way to the next section of ice-free transect.
If you include these data, you bias your estimates towards near-ice
densities.

Steve
